summary: A cell-level block of colonic mucosa: a flat surface epithelium dipping into two straight crypts (of Lieberkuhn), lined by simple columnar absorptive cells and many goblet cells, each crypt wrapped in its basement membrane and set in lamina propria. The face you open on is cut through the crypts lengthwise to show their lining.
clinical: Most colorectal cancers arise from the crypt epithelium, typically through an adenomatous polyp (adenoma-carcinoma sequence); invasion is defined by tumour crossing the muscularis mucosae below the crypts.
Chronic inflammation confined to the mucosa distorts and branches the crypts, depletes goblet cells and produces crypt abscesses - the key biopsy features.

SubTool-2.name: Absorptive columnar cells
SubTool-2.description: Tall simple columnar cells (colonocytes) with oval basal nuclei, covering the surface and lining the crypts. Their main job is absorbing water and sodium, which dries the faecal stream; they have only a short, sparse brush border compared with small-intestinal enterocytes.

SubTool-3.name: Goblet cells
SubTool-3.description: Pale, mucin-filled cells with a compressed nucleus at their narrow base. They are far more numerous in the colon than in the small intestine and crowd the crypt walls; their mucus lubricates the drying faeces and forms the protective mucus layer over the epithelium.

SubTool-0.name: Basement membrane
SubTool-0.description: The thin sheet on which the epithelium rests, shaped here as a sleeve around each crypt (shown semi-transparent so the crypt lining shows through) that flares out beneath the surface epithelium. Every colonic epithelial cell touches it, which is what makes the epithelium simple; it separates the epithelium from the lamina propria.

SubTool-1.name: Basement membrane
SubTool-1.description: The thin sheet on which the epithelium rests, shaped here as a sleeve around each crypt (shown semi-transparent so the crypt lining shows through) that flares out beneath the surface epithelium. Every colonic epithelial cell touches it, which is what makes the epithelium simple; it separates the epithelium from the lamina propria.

SubTool-4.name: Lamina propria
SubTool-4.description: Loose connective tissue filling the spaces between the crypts, shown see-through so the crypts can be seen inside it. It carries capillaries, lymphocytes and plasma cells; lymphatics are scarce here, so carcinoma confined to the mucosa almost never metastasises.

notes: Parts identified from focused renders: SubTool-2 = pink columnar cells with elongated nuclei (colonocytes; a few pale cells are also baked into this mesh), SubTool-3 = pale mint cells with basal nuclei (goblet cells), SubTool-0/1 = one sleeve per crypt (basement membrane, merged; set to alpha 0.5 because from the uncut side these opaque sleeves hid the crypt epithelium), SubTool-4 = the translucent block around everything (lamina propria; alpha lowered from 0.66 to 0.3). Stem, enteroendocrine and other crypt-base cells are not modelled separately. The model's cut face is at -z, so the opening view is yaw 180 rather than rotating the geometry. Vertex colours look sRGB-encoded but are read as linear by the importer, so the whole model renders paler than the creator's thumbnail; per-part colour overrides were not used because they would erase the painted nuclei.
